description: We are a team of 5 third-year high school students from the Magshimim Cyber program with strong skills in programming, software, and analytical problem-solving. We chose the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge because it combines lunar exploration, data visualization, and technical engineering in a way that fits our interests well.
summary:
MMildeum is an interactive web application that helps users explore and compare potential lunar landing sites, with a focus on the Moon’s south pole. Developed for the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge, it brings NASA terrain data and astronomical calculations together to make lunar mission planning easier to understand.
Users can investigate surface elevation, slope, and roughness, alongside the positions of the Sun and Earth for selected locations and dates. These factors help users understand the trade-offs between suitable terrain, access to sunlight for solar power, and opportunities for direct communication with Earth.
By presenting complex data through interactive maps and visualizations, MMildeum makes it easier to explore why one location or mission date may be more promising than another. The project turns lunar datasets into an accessible tool for students, space enthusiasts, and early exploration of mission scenarios.
details:
MMildeum helps users explore potential lunar landing sites and understand how terrain, sunlight, and Earth visibility affect mission planning. Our focus is the lunar south pole, where choosing a location involves balancing several competing requirements.

How it works

Users select lunar coordinates and a date to investigate conditions at a potential landing site. The application combines terrain analysis, including elevation, slope, and surface roughness, with calculations of the Sun’s and Earth’s positions. Interactive maps and visualizations bring these results together so users can explore different locations and dates.

We use NASA Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) data to examine the lunar surface and JPL Horizons for astronomical position calculations. These sources help connect the physical characteristics of a site with questions about solar power and direct-to-Earth communication.

Tools and development

The project uses Python for backend calculations and data processing, alongside JavaScript, HTML, and CSS for the browser interface. Rasterio supports processing of lunar raster datasets, while Astroquery provides access to astronomical data services. Our mapping tools include OpenLayers and CesiumJS for exploring the lunar surface.

Our approach

The project’s central idea is to bring several aspects of landing-site evaluation into one interactive workflow. A location with relatively gentle terrain may have less favorable lighting or communication conditions. Examining these factors together helps users understand the trade-offs instead of judging a site from a single measurement.

During development, we considered terrain variability, changes in astronomical geometry over time, dataset resolution, and the clarity of the interface. We also distinguish between different terrain measurements: elevation, slope, and roughness describe different properties and should not be treated as interchangeable.

Benefits and intended impact

MMildeum makes lunar datasets more accessible to students, educators, and space enthusiasts. It supports early exploration of mission scenarios and helps explain why selecting a landing site requires more than finding a flat area on a map. It is an exploratory prototype, intended to support learning and comparison rather than certify landing safety.
